claims.claim: Le Guin praises in Goblin Secrets a haunting quality, a sense of depth, of unspoken further implication in the adventures and the characters.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, blog 52, 'Some Recent Fantasies', 21 May 2012
claims.quote: a sense of depth, of unspoken further implication

claims.claim: Le Guin says she likes stories that take the reader quietly into a place and let them do difficult and interesting work with some of the people there.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, blog 52, 'Some Recent Fantasies', 21 May 2012
claims.quote: take you quietly into a place and let you do difficult

claims.claim: Le Guin says Homer truly does not take sides, and that this is what permits the story to be tragic.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, blog 31, 'Papa H', 24 July 2011

claims.claim: Le Guin says Homer's impartiality is far from dispassionate, the story being a torrent of passionate actions while remaining unprejudiced.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, blog 31, 'Papa H', 24 July 2011
claims.quote: His impartiality is far from dispassionate

claims.claim: Le Guin says she had put clues into A Wizard of Earthsea without knowing it, and that they led her on into Ged's life.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, interview in Karabatak Magazine, 9th edition, summer 2013
claims.quote: I had put clues into the book, without knowing it

claims.claim: Le Guin says the rhythms of a prose work are a very long beat, different from and in a way much coarser than the rhythms of poetry.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin in conversation with David Naimon, 'Dictators are Always Afraid of Poets', excerpt from Conversations on Writing (Tin House, 2018), Literary Hub
claims.quote: long beat, the rhythms of a prose work
claims.page: the exchange about Virginia Woolf and sound

claims.claim: Rich Horton reports that the ethnographic sections of Always Coming Home, while intellectually interesting, are often a struggle to read.
claims.source: Rich Horton, "Review: Always Coming Home, by Ursula K. Le Guin", Strange at Ecbatan blog, 24 April 2024
claims.quote: intellectually intriguing, but, really, often a struggle to read

claims.feature: other: archival register as a whole book
claims.claim: Horton describes Always Coming Home as reading to a great extent like a writer deciding to include all her notes.
claims.source: Rich Horton, Strange at Ecbatan blog, 24 April 2024
claims.quote: like a writer deciding to include all her notes

claims.claim: Horton judges Always Coming Home more impressive than involving.
claims.source: Rich Horton, Strange at Ecbatan blog, 24 April 2024
claims.quote: more impressive than it is involving

claims.claim: Horton records that Le Guin placed a roughly hundred-page appendix called The Back of the Book at the end of the novel.
claims.source: Rich Horton, Strange at Ecbatan blog, 24 April 2024
claims.quote: in the final section, some 100 pages

claims.claim: Horton identifies the Pandora sections as the voice of the author or the future anthropologist recording the material.
claims.source: Rich Horton, Strange at Ecbatan blog, 24 April 2024
claims.quote: a stand in for the author or the future anthropologist

claims.claim: Scott Manley Hadley describes Always Coming Home as a novel that masquerades as anthropology, a study of a people.
claims.source: Scott Manley Hadley, "Always Coming Home by Ursula Le Guin", Triumph Of The Now, 13 July 2019
claims.quote: a novel that masquerades as anthropology, a study of a people

claims.claim: Hadley reports that Le Guin includes third-person essays on Kesh culture covering how they measure time and how they draw maps.
claims.source: Scott Manley Hadley, Triumph Of The Now, 13 July 2019
claims.quote: how they measure time, how they draw maps

claims.claim: Hadley calls Always Coming Home fiction without being storytelling, though it contains many stories.
claims.source: Scott Manley Hadley, Triumph Of The Now, 13 July 2019
claims.quote: It is fiction without being storytelling, though it contains many

claims.claim: Cat Eldridge contrasts the two worlds: Tolkien has virtually no ethnographic detail where Le Guin has no history.
claims.source: Cat Eldridge, review of Always Coming Home, A Green Man Review
claims.quote: Tolkien’s world has virtually no ethnographic detail
